narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: Compare four selected roles, not four fixed personalities: Achilles facing grief, Odysseus recognised at home, Heracles serving Eurystheus, and Theseus founding civic order. Each contrast needs evidence from its own work.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the source does
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translation; whitespace normalized): “others looked one to another and marvelled also, but Priam besought Achilles saying, “Think of your father, O Achilles like unto the gods, who is such even as I am, on the sad threshold of old age. It may be that those who dwell near him harass him, and there is none to keep war and ruin from him. Yet”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Interpretation: The point of comparison is not to rank them but to see how each source constructs value and consequence.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Check all four references before making the comparison. An Iliad passage can support a claim about Achilles, but it cannot by itself establish Penelope’s test, Heracles’ service, or Theseus’ civic role.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: Carry this method into the next programme: compare without flattening.

quiz.prompt: Why does this comparison need more than an Iliad citation?

choices.text: The Iliad contains every surviving heroic narrative.
A comparison has no factual claims to support.
Claims about the other heroes require their own source passages.

quiz.explanation: Claims about the other heroes require their own source passages. is the passage-specific answer. Check The Iliad (Book 24, Priam appeals to Achilles); Bibliotheca (Library) (Library 2.4.12, oracle assigns service); The Odyssey (Book 23, Odysseus explains the rooted bed); Plutarch: Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (Life of Theseus, unification of Attica), keeping each work and version distinct.
